sentences: The encounter with the stranger — from another people, another culture, another way of being — has always evoked mixed feelings: curiosity and fear, fascination and rejection, attraction and unease.
The stranger disturbs us because he is strange, because he embodies a way of being different from our own, which calls into question what we took for granted.
And yet, this encounter that disturbs us is also what reveals us, enriches us, and helps us grow.
Questioning our relationship with the stranger, with strangeness, is to understand both what we fear and what we gain in meeting the other.
What do we fear in the stranger?
His difference, first and foremost, which unsettles us.
The stranger embodies a way of being other than our own, which shows that our way is not the only one, that it is neither obvious nor necessary.
This revelation is unsettling: it shakes our certainties, relativizes our obviousness, deprives us of the comfort of believing that our way of life is the only natural one.
The stranger, by his mere existence, calls into question what we took for granted; and this questioning, while fruitful, is also unsettling.
We fear the stranger because he threatens our certainties, because he forces us to recognize the relativity of what we believed to be absolute.
We also fear the stranger as a threat, whether real or imaginary, to our identity, our security, our world.
This fear can have real foundations when the encounter is conflictual; but it is often exaggerated, fueled by imagination, projected onto the stranger who becomes the receptacle of our fears.
The stranger is easily transformed into a threat, a scapegoat, an embodiment of everything that worries us; their difference is perceived as a danger, their otherness as an aggression.
This fear of the stranger, when it is not controlled, leads to rejection, hostility, hatred, and the worst violence committed in the name of self-defense against the other.
But if the stranger disturbs us and frightens us, they are also what reveals and enriches us.
For their difference, which destabilizes our certainties, is also what makes us see them, relativizes them, and frees us from them.

By encountering another way of being, we discover that ours is just one way among many, and this discovery, while unsettling, is also liberating: it frees us from being trapped in a single vision, opens us to the diversity of ways of being human, and makes us broader.
The stranger is a mirror that reveals us to ourselves, showing us what is particular about us; they are a window onto other worlds, which expands our own.
What disturbs us in them is also what enriches us.
There is more.
Strangeness is not only found outside, in another people, another culture; it is also within us, closer than we think.
We are strangers to ourselves, as a thinker once said, carrying within us a part of shadow, the unknown, strangeness, that we do not control.

Recognizing the strangeness within oneself may be the condition for welcoming that of others: for the one who rejects all strangeness, who desires purity, an identity without mixture, the same without the other, that person rejects the stranger outside just as they repress the strangeness within.
Welcoming the other implies accepting one's own part of strangeness, renouncing the fantasy of a pure identity, and recognizing that we ourselves are traversed by otherness.
Our relationship with the stranger is thus revealing of who we are.

Fearing them, rejecting them, making them a scapegoat, is to yield to fear, to refuse the questioning they bring, to shut oneself in an identity that seeks to be pure; welcoming them, opening up to their difference, accepting to be destabilized, is to demonstrate a strength and generosity that enrich.

The encounter with the stranger is a test, which reveals whether we are capable of welcoming what disturbs us, allowing ourselves to be questioned, enriching ourselves with difference, or if we retreat into fear and rejection.

And for those who have learned a foreign language, entering a world different from their own, this test has already been faced and overcome: for learning the language of the stranger is already to welcome them, to open oneself to their world, to allow oneself to be enriched by their difference.
Learning a language may be the most beautiful response to the fear of the stranger: not the rejection of what disturbs us, but the welcoming of what enriches us.

sentences: Last night, the home team won an extraordinary match in the final seconds of the game.
The stadium had been full since early afternoon, and thousands of supporters had been waiting for this match for weeks.
The atmosphere was electric as soon as the players entered the field.
The start of the match was difficult for the home team.
The opponent scored a goal in the tenth minute, and the supporters remained silent for a long time.
The local players seemed nervous and struggled to control the ball during the first half of the match.
During the break, the coach spoke at length with his players in the locker room.
He reminded them of the importance of this match for the standings and asked them to stay calm and focused.
This speech clearly changed something, as the team returned to the field with much more energy.
When they returned from the locker room, the game completely changed.
The home players started to dominate the ball and create many scoring opportunities.
The young striker of the team, only nineteen years old, equalized the score with a powerful shot from outside the penalty area.
The stadium erupted with joy.
The match remained very tight until the last minutes.
Both teams had chances to score, but the goalkeepers made excellent saves.
Everyone thought the match would end in a draw, which would have been an honorable result for both teams.
But in stoppage time, in the ninety-third minute, the same young striker received a perfect cross and scored a beautiful header.
The stadium went wild.
The supporters cheered with joy for several minutes, and some even cried tears of happiness at this historic moment for the club.
After the match, the coach explained to the journalists that his players never gave up, even after conceding the first goal.
He also praised the young striker for his outstanding performance and announced that he would play an even more important role in the upcoming matches.
The next match will take place next Sunday, against one of the best teams in the league.
The supporters are already hoping to relive the same emotions and continue to celebrate this memorable victory in the streets of the city late into the night.
For the club, this victory is also important financially.
Winning this match allows them to stay at the top of the standings and hope for a place in European competition next season, which would bring a lot of money and visibility to the team.

sentences: And this is what has emboldened you, Maximilien; this is what gives me both a sweet and a bitter life, to the point that I often wonder which is better for me: the sorrow that my stepmother's harshness and her blind preference for her child caused me in the past, or the happiness filled with dangers that I experience when I see you.
Danger!
Maximilien exclaimed; can you say such a harsh and unjust word?
Have you ever seen a more submissive slave than me?
You have allowed me to speak to you sometimes, Valentine, but you have forbidden me to follow you; I have obeyed.

Since I found a way to slip into this enclosure, to talk with you through this door, to be finally so close to you without seeing you, have I ever, tell me, asked to touch the hem of your dress through these bars?
Have I ever taken a step to cross this wall, a ridiculous obstacle for my youth and strength?
Never a reproach about your strictness, never a desire openly expressed; I have been bound to my word like a knight of old.
Admit at least this, so that I do not think you unjust.
It's true, said Valentine, as she passed between two boards the tip of one of her slender fingers on which Maximilien placed his lips; it's true, you are an honest friend.
But in the end, you acted only out of self-interest, my dear Maximilien; you knew very well that from the day the slave became demanding, he would have to lose everything.

You promised me the friendship of a brother, to me who has no friends, to me whom my father forgets, to me whom my stepmother persecutes, and who has for consolation only the old man who is motionless, mute, frozen, whose hand cannot hold mine, whose eye alone can speak to me, and whose heart undoubtedly still beats for me with a remnant of warmth.
Bitter mockery of fate that makes me an enemy and a victim of all those who are stronger than me, and gives me a corpse for support and for a friend!
Oh!
truly, Maximilien, I repeat it to you, I am very unhappy, and you are right to love me for who I am and not for yourself.

A loud voice shouted, "Here are some friends!" And Mathieu appeared in the doorway.
He was a sixty-year-old man, thin, with a goatee and long white mustaches.
My companion shook his hand, introduced me, and Mathieu welcomed us into a cool kitchen that also served as his dining room.

sentences: This sentiment is worthy of the father of peoples, Mentor replied; it is to this kindness, and not to the vain magnificence of your city, that I recognize in you the heart of a true king.
But you must safeguard your honor, for the very interest of your kingdom.

They will have no trouble understanding that this war requires numerous troops.
Thus, they will agree that you should initially provide them only with a small support against the Daunians.
At these words, Idomeneus appeared like a man relieved of a heavy burden.
You save, dear friend, he said to Mentor, my honor, and the reputation of this fledgling city, whose exhaustion you will hide from all my neighbors.

But what appearance is there in saying that I want to send troops to Ithaca to restore Ulysses, or at least Telemachus his son, while Telemachus himself is engaged in going to war against the Daunians!
At these words, Idomeneus exclaimed: Happy is the king who is supported by wise counsel!
A wise and loyal friend is worth more to a king than victorious armies.
But doubly happy is the king who feels his happiness and knows how to benefit from it through the proper use of wise counsel!
For it often happens that one distances from his trust wise and virtuous men whose virtue he fears, to lend an ear to flatterers whom he does not fear for their treachery.

He went to find the officers to find out, as he said, why they had taken his man away.

SINCE his entry into France with the invading army, Walter Schnaffs considered himself the most unfortunate man.
He was big, walked with difficulty, breathed heavily, and suffered terribly from his very flat and very fat feet.

He was also peaceful and kind-hearted, by no means magnanimous or bloodthirsty, a father of four children whom he adored and married to a young blonde woman, whose tenderness, little attentions, and kisses he desperately missed every evening.
He loved to get up late and go to bed early, eat good food slowly, and drink beer in the breweries.

He also thought that everything sweet in life disappears with death; and he harbored a terrible hatred, both instinctive and rational, in his heart for cannons, rifles, revolvers, and sabers, but especially for bayonets, feeling incapable of maneuvering that quick weapon well enough to defend his big belly.

And when he lay down on the ground at night, rolled up in his coat next to the comrades who were snoring, he thought long and hard about his loved ones left behind and the dangers scattered along his path:--If he were killed, what would happen to the little ones?
Who would feed and raise them?
At that very moment, they were not rich, despite the debts he had incurred when leaving to leave them some money.
And Walter Schnaffs sometimes cried.
At the beginning of battles, he felt such weakness in his legs that he would have fallen down if he hadn't thought that the entire army would pass over his body.
The whistling of the bullets made the hair on his skin stand on end.

sentences: However, as if crossing the ice fields had been feasible, preparations for departure were actively continuing at the trading post.

Nothing should be overlooked for the safety of the expedition; everything had to be anticipated, and one had to reckon not only with difficulties and fatigue, but also with the whims of this polar nature, which fiercely defends itself against human exploration.
The dog teams had received special attention.
They were allowed to run around the fort so that the exercise would restore their somewhat stiffened strength from a long rest.
Overall, these animals were all in satisfactory condition and could, if not overworked, manage a long trek.
The sleds were carefully inspected.
The rough surface of the icefield would inevitably expose them to violent shocks.
Thus, they had to be reinforced in their main parts, their lower chassis, their curved front runners, etc.
This task rightfully belonged to carpenter Mac Nap and his men, who made these vehicles as sturdy as possible.
In addition, two large sled-carts were constructed, one intended for transporting provisions and the other for transporting furs.
These carts were to be pulled by domestic reindeer, and they were perfectly suited for this purpose.
The furs were, it must be agreed, a luxury cargo that perhaps wasn't wise to carry.

But Jasper Hobson wanted, as much as possible, to safeguard the interests of the Hudson's Bay Company, being determined, moreover, to abandon these furs along the way if they compromised or hindered the caravan's progress.
There was no risk, moreover, since these precious furs, if left in the trading post's stores, would inevitably be lost.
As for the provisions, that was another matter.
The supplies had to be abundant and easily transportable.
One could not rely in any way on the products of the hunt.
Edible game, as soon as the passage became feasible, would take the lead and would soon have rallied to the southern regions.

Therefore, preserved meats, corned beef, hare pâtés, dried fish, biscuits, of which the supply was unfortunately quite limited, etc., ample reserves of sorrel and other provisions, brandy, spirits for making hot drinks, etc., were placed in a special cart.
Jasper Hobson would have liked to bring fuel, for during six hundred miles, he would find neither a tree, nor a bush, nor moss, and one could not count on wreckage or wood washed up by the sea.
But such a burden could not be accepted, and he had to give up on it.
Fortunately, warm clothing would not be lacking; there would be plenty, comfortable, and if necessary, they could draw furs from the cart.

How funny it would be to find myself among people who walk upside down.

In the Antipodes, I believe." (She wasn't upset this time that there was no one there to hear her, as that word didn't seem quite right to her.) "Oh, but I will have to ask them the name of the country.--Excuse me, madam, is this New Zealand or Australia?"--At the same time, she tried to curtsy.
(What an idea!
Curtsying in the air!
Tell me, how would you go about it?) 'What a little ignoramus!' the lady will think when I ask her this question.

No, I shouldn't ask that; perhaps I'll see it written somewhere." Falling, falling, falling!--So Alice, having nothing better to do, started talking to herself: "Dinah will notice my absence this evening, of course." (Dinah was her cat.) "I hope they don't forget to give her her bowl of milk at tea time.
Dinah, my dear, why aren't you here with me?
There are no mice in the air, I'm afraid; but you could catch a bat, and that looks a lot like a mouse, you know.
But do cats eat bats?" Here sleep began to overtake Alice.
She kept repeating, half asleep: "Do cats eat bats?
Do cats eat bats?" And sometimes: "Do bats eat cats?" Because you see, since she couldn't answer either of those questions, it didn't matter how she asked them.

She was dozing off and began to dream that she was walking along holding Dinah's hand, very seriously saying to her: "Come on, Dinah, tell me the truth, have you ever eaten bats?" When suddenly, poof!
there she was lying on a pile of sticks and dry leaves,--and she had finished falling.
Alice hadn't hurt herself at all.
Quickly she got back on her feet and looked up; but everything was dark up there.
She saw in front of her a long passage and the White Rabbit running at full speed.

There wasn't a moment to lose; Alice took off like the wind and just arrived in time to hear the Rabbit say, as he turned the corner: "By my whiskers and ears, how late it is!" She was only two steps away: but as soon as he turned the corner, the Rabbit had disappeared.
She then found herself in a long, low room, lit by a row of lamps hanging from the ceiling.

So I say it, so I proclaim it aloud: yes, sir, you were right to take revenge on my father, and I, his son, thank you for not having done more!” The thunder that fell among the spectators of this unexpected scene would not have astonished them more than this declaration from Albert.

As for Monte-Cristo, his eyes had slowly turned to heaven with an expression of infinite gratitude, and he could not help but admire how this fiery nature of Albert, whose courage he had known well among the Roman bandits, had suddenly bent to this sudden humiliation.
He also recognized the influence of Mercédès and understood how this noble heart had not opposed the sacrifice that she had known in advance would be in vain.
“Now, sir,” Albert said, “if you find that the apologies I have just made to you are sufficient, your hand, please.
After the rare merit of infallibility that seems to be yours, the first of all merits, in my opinion, is to know how to admit one's faults.
But this admission concerns me alone.
I acted rightly according to men, but you, you acted rightly according to God.
Only an angel could save one of us from death, and the angel descended from heaven, if not to make us two friends, alas!
